decisions.decision: The period registry gets a merge order: subscriptions, debts and incomes are re-keyed before categories, and after the merge any version at or after its row's end is deleted; a category whose only referrers the reopen removed is deleted with them.
decisions.why: A review step 3 leftover: after a reopen a version could sit at the end (never in force) or a void category remain.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 4 database, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: An ended debt is frozen
decisions.decision: Once a debt has ended, its payments cannot be added, changed or deleted and its adjustments cannot be added or deleted (debt_ended); its remaining amount stays as it was when it ended.
decisions.why: Ending a debt keeps its history (R-DEBT-113); changing it afterwards would change a closed record nobody looks at.
rejected: Allowing payments dated in the periods the debt was in force.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 4 database, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: A debt's paid share
decisions.decision: debt_overview.paid_percent is the payments over principal plus interest plus adjustments, a whole percent rounded down, 100 exactly when nothing remains, 0 while nothing has been paid (and when the total owed is not positive with nothing paid).
decisions.why: Rounding down never shows 100 % for a debt that still owes a rappen.
rejected: Payments over principal only: interest would let it exceed 100 % while still owing.
source: owner-request: coordinator addendum to the step 4 database review (screens asks), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The database gives the total still owed
decisions.decision: A view debt_totals gives per budget the sum of the positive remaining amounts of its debts in force and the number still owing; overpaid and paid-off debts add nothing.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-110: the client no longer adds amounts up (C-LOGIC-003), and an overpaid debt cannot hide another's debt.
rejected: Adding up debt_overview.remaining in the client (D-191).
source: owner-request: coordinator addendum to the step 4 database review (screens asks), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Hot helper functions are plpgsql
decisions.decision: Helpers called per row or per period by the views (totals, spans, reading_seq, the projection) are plpgsql, so their plans are kept for the session; a SQL function with a search_path setting is planned again on each call. A lookup that a generic plan would scan sequentially disables sequential scans in the function rather than forcing custom plans.
decisions.why: The pages at the limits (50 subscriptions, 50 debts, 200 categories, 120 periods) must read in about 250 ms.
rejected: force_custom_plan: one planning per call again.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 4 database, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Changing a transaction and its link in one call
decisions.decision: update_transaction takes p_relink: with it, p_debt_id and p_subscription_id (both null: no link) replace the link in the same call, checked against the new fields; without it the link is kept as before.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-111: a payment is never left half-changed by a failure between calls.
rejected: Keeping three calls (D-194).
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 4 database, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The database gives the terms in force in a chosen period
decisions.decision: get_subscription_terms, get_debt_terms, get_category_terms and get_income_terms (record id, period id) return the terms of the record in force in that period, the period they took effect (terms_from_period_id) and the first period of the next existing change or of its end (until_period_id), so a correction form starts from them without reading the version tables and can say up to which period the correction applies.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-130: the rule "the version with the greatest effective_from_seq not after the period" stays in the database (C-LOGIC-001, C-LOGIC-003); D-210's client lookup can be replaced by these calls.
rejected: A column per period on the overviews: one row per record and period would multiply the views.
source: owner-request: coordinator addendum to the step 4 database review (screens asks), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The database says beforehand what a removal from a chosen period does
decisions.decision: preview_end_subscription and preview_remove_debt (record id, period id; null: the current period) answer what end_subscription / remove_debt from that period would do now: deleted, ended, or the refusal's code, with the same conditions as the writes.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-131: removal_deletes covers a removal from now only; the dialogs of D-214 can say the one outcome that applies for an earlier period.
source: owner-request: coordinator addendum to the step 4 database review (screens asks), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Corrections read the terms of their period from the database
decisions.decision: The correction forms (incomes, categories, subscriptions, debts) read the terms in force in the period chosen with get_income_terms, get_category_terms, get_subscription_terms and get_debt_terms, show them as the starting values, say how far the correction reaches (until_period_id), offer no save when the record was not in force there, and send only what the user changes. The client no longer reads the version tables.
decisions.why: D-219 gives these terms in the database (C-LOGIC-001); the client's own lookup of the version tables (D-210) was the one place it chose a version itself.
rejected: Keeping the version-table lookup (D-210): it duplicated the database's choice of version.
source: owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens review round 2, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: A long absence is caught up in words, without progress
decisions.decision: While a very long absence is caught up, the app shows only "Catching up on the time since your last visit…" and a short explanation, no progress bar and no figure, then loads the pages.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-121 by default: ensure_periods says how many periods it made, not how many remain, so a bar would invent its end; a step takes up to about 3 s plus its commit (D-276), and a long absence a few steps.
rejected: A progress bar from the periods made so far: the total is unknown.
source: owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens review round 2, 2026-11-16
owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens adapted to the database re-review and step 5, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The debt chart reads up to 10 000 events
decisions.decision: The debt page reads get_debt_history 1000 rows a page; the chart reads pages by itself until the history ends or 10 000 events, and then says where it stops; the table shows 50 rows at a time, oldest first (the order the database pages in), reading the next page when its rows are shown.
decisions.why: A debt with 20 000 payments must not freeze the page, and the chart of an ordinary debt must show all of it; ten pages are about 2 MB and a few hundred milliseconds.
rejected: Reading the whole history whatever its size: a very long one would be read and drawn at once.
The table newest first: the database pages oldest first only (Q-141).
source: owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens review round 2, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Back to the schedule from the database's preview
decisions.decision: The periods page asks preview_move_period_start when the menu of a period whose previous end was set by hand opens: it offers the move with the start it would give when accepted, disabled with the refusal in words when not, and nothing when already on the schedule.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-091, with R-PERIOD-133: the client offers only what the database would accept and names its date.
source: owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens review round 2, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Three reads, one per view, built on the progress code
decisions.decision: get_period_trend (one row per period), get_category_trend (one row per category line and period) and get_period_comparison (a 'total' row, then one row per category) answer each comparison view in one call. Their figures are read from period_summaries and private.category_progress, the code behind get_period_progress, so they cannot disagree with the progress view. Averages, differences, lengths and the range's flags are columns, repeated where a view needs them on every row.
decisions.why: One implementation of every figure (C-LOGIC-001), nothing for the client to compute (C-LOGIC-003), and typed rows the generated types describe.
rejected: JSON documents: untyped for the client.
Separate calls for the totals and the averages: more than one call per view.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 5 database (period comparison), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Averages over the completed periods, rounded half away from zero
decisions.decision: An average is the sum over the completed periods of the range divided by their number, rounded to the rappen with halves away from zero (also for a negative result); null when none is completed. The average result is the average of the results, so it can differ by a rappen from the average income minus the average spent. A category's average spent divides by every completed period of the range, including those where it was not in force (they count what was spent, usually nothing).
decisions.why: The running period is incomplete and would pull averages down; one rounding rule for all averages; a category's average is comparable with the trend's.
rejected: Averaging a category only over the periods it was in force (Q-160).
Banker's rounding: unusual for amounts shown to people.
source: owner-request: database developer decision for step 5, within the coordinator's brief, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Empty versus zero in the comparison
decisions.decision: planned is empty when the category is not in force in the period (the progress view's expected 0 means nothing planned because it does not exist then). In the trend, a period without a progress row for a line is not in force, spent 0, committed 0. Side by side, a period where the category has no progress row is empty on every figure; the differences count an empty side as nothing spent or committed, and planned_difference is empty unless both plan something. There is no uncategorised line: an expense or refund always has a category.
decisions.why: The brief asks that "not in force" and "nothing spent" stay distinct; the difference must stay a number so the lines add up to the totals' difference.
source: owner-request: database developer decision for step 5, within the coordinator's brief, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Range of 1 to 24 periods; catching up first
decisions.decision: p_count accepts 1 to 24 (12 by default; the screens offer 6, 12 and 24), invalid_limit otherwise. The range ends at the current period, or at the last one once the budget has ended. The reads catch up like get_current_period; when a very long absence is not yet caught up they raise catching_up (the bounded catch-up of that call is not kept, the client calls ensure_periods until it returns 0, as my_budgets.caught_up says).
decisions.why: 24 periods at the limits answer within the time budget; a range that silently stopped years before today would mislead.
rejected: Answering the periods that exist so far: a trend that ends years ago without saying so.
source: owner-request: database developer decision for step 5, within the coordinator's brief, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Every read fits in one API response, or is paged
decisions.decision: The API returns at most 1000 rows per request (max_rows, not raised) and cuts a longer answer silently. So: get_category_trend returns one row per category line with the per-period figures as arrays aligned with its period_ids (the periods of get_period_trend with the same p_count); a budget holds at most 900 categories, 900 subscriptions and 900 debts, void rows included (the earlier limits of D-153 and D-180, which do not count void rows, stay; this bound only stops a budget accumulating void rows without end); the periods are read with list_periods, newest first, at most 200 a page; preview_reopen lists at most 1000 rows, the 1000th saying how many more changes there are. Every other read is bounded below 1000 by a limit (see docs/database.md).
decisions.why: Coordinator finding: 42 lines over 24 periods already passed 1000 rows, and the limits gave 4800; the screen would have drawn a partial answer without an error. Void rows are kept only for their transactions and were not counted, so without a bound the category, subscription and debt reads could pass 1000 too.
rejected: Raising max_rows: the cut stays, only further away.
Counting void rows in the 500 / 200 limits: reopens D-153 and D-180 for a case only abuse reaches.
Paging every per-category read: the comparison and progress views must add up within one answer.
source: owner-request: coordinator finding on the step 5 database (API row limit), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: No call does an unbounded catch-up
decisions.decision: A catch-up step creates at most 120 periods with their interest and charges (D-276 also bounds its time). ensure_periods and get_current_period do one step and keep it; my_budgets.caught_up says whether more remains, and the client calls ensure_periods until it returns 0. Every other read, preview and write (all of them through private.read_catch_up, private.current_period or private.lock_and_catch_up) does at most one step and, when the budget is still behind, answers catching_up and changes nothing (its step is rolled back with it). A write no longer catches up in full. Step 2's period_generation_runaway error stays gone. Supersedes D-201.
decisions.why: Re-review finding 1: seven previews created every missing period in one call (480 after 40 years) and timed out over HTTP, and catching_up was never answered. A write catching up in full would hit the statement timeout at the limits.
rejected: Writes catching up in full: the statement timeout at the limits.
Raising the step size: the same cliff later.
source: owner-request: coordinator, independent re-review of the step 4 database fixes, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: A held-back charge blocks schedule changes
decisions.decision: While a subscription's next scheduled date has come and its charge is held back by the transaction limit, update_subscription refuses a change of cadence or a next charge date (from now or as a correction) and end_subscription refuses to end it, with charge_held_back, changing nothing; preview_end_subscription says so as its refusal. A name, price or category change is allowed: the held charge is created, once there is room, with the terms in force in its own period, so it cannot be lost. subscription_overview.next_charge_date shows the held date meanwhile.
decisions.why: Re-review finding 3: a cadence change while a charge waited moved the schedule past the held date, so the charge was never created (R-SUBSCRIPTION-112: none skipped).
rejected: Creating the held charge at the moment of the edit: the budget has no room for it.
source: owner-request: coordinator, independent re-review of the step 4 database fixes, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Interest on the balance before the period, at period creation; the projection and "never"
decisions.decision: A period's interest for a debt is computed when the period is created, on the debt's balance from everything dated before the period's start (its opening, payments, adjustments and earlier interest), whatever day the catch-up runs, as one twelfth of the yearly rate rounded half up to the rappen, as an entry of that period in the debt's history (dated at the period's start). A debt whose opened_on is not before the period's start gets no interest for that period; its first comes with the next one, so the history always starts with the opening. It is computed once: a payment or adjustment back-dated later does not recompute it (an adjustment exists for that). It is applied exactly once per debt and period however the period came to exist; a reopen that merges a period removes its entry and creating the period again computes it by the same rule, so redoing without other changes gives the same amount. No interest on a balance of zero or less. A planned payment less than or equal to one period's interest means the debt never ends; the projection has a horizon of 600 periods (50 years). Supersedes D-172.
decisions.why: Re-review finding 4: interest on the balance at the moment of the catch-up gave an entry dated before the opening (an early pay date) and a different amount for a period created again after a payment dated inside it. The projection already assumes this rule (each period's interest on what remains after the previous period).
rejected: The balance at the moment of creation: depends on the day the catch-up runs.
source: owner-request: coordinator, independent re-review of the step 4 database fixes, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: No terms where a record is not in force
decisions.decision: get_subscription_terms, get_debt_terms, get_category_terms and get_income_terms answer in_force false and every term, terms_from_period_id and until_period_id null for a period where the record is not in force (before it starts, from its end on), so a correction form cannot offer to correct a period the record does not cover.
decisions.why: Re-review: from the end period on the last terms came back with in_force false, which the form could have offered to correct.
source: owner-request: coordinator, independent re-review of the step 4 database fixes, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The transactions list says which payments are frozen
decisions.decision: transaction_list has debt_ended: true for a payment of a debt that has ended (it cannot be changed, unlinked or deleted, D-209), false otherwise. Nothing is frozen for an ended subscription: its charges can still be edited, confirmed, dismissed or deleted, so there is no subscription counterpart.
decisions.why: Screens round 2 (Q-140): the list read debt_overview to know which payments were frozen.

decisions.title: A debt's history newest first
decisions.decision: get_debt_history takes p_newest_first (default false): the same rows newest first, the four-part cursor (date, kind, created_at, entry_id) then continuing towards older rows; balance is computed over the whole history in the oldest-first order, so it is the same in both directions.
decisions.why: Screens round 2 (Q-141): the history table starts with the latest events.

decisions.title: A catch-up step's work is bounded in time too
decisions.decision: A step stops creating periods after about two seconds of work (at least one period per call), then creates the charges due in what it created. Measured locally with 50 subscriptions and 50 debts with interest after 100 years: statement at most 3.0 s, commit at most 0.6 s, 44 to 120 periods per step; a period costs about three times more at 1200 periods of history than at 120 (deferred checks and the budget's transactions), so the time bound, not the period bound, keeps each step under the 8 s statement timeout.
decisions.why: Re-review: the tenth 120-period step after 100 years took 11.6 s over HTTP.
rejected: A fixed smaller step: still unbounded in time as the history grows.
source: owner-request: coordinator, independent re-review of the step 4 database fixes, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: One import, in batches of idempotent chunks
decisions.decision: private.import_plan decides what each row does and private.import_apply does it; preview_import, import_transactions, import_with_token and import_skipped_anyway all use them. Rows are JSON objects (date, amount in integer rappen, direction, description, merchant, bank_transaction_id, hint, details, and a member's action, kind, category). A batch has an id the caller generates and up to 100 chunks of up to 500 rows (50 000 rows); a chunk sent again answers as the first time and records nothing. A chunk is all or nothing, refused before anything is written when the transaction limit cannot hold it (detail: how many would fit).
decisions.why: The write must equal the preview, and a statement larger than one answer (R-APP-170) must survive a lost response without double imports.
rejected: A server-generated batch id: a retried first call would open a second batch.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The merchant key and merchant rules
decisions.decision: The database computes a row's merchant key: its merchant field, else its description, lower-cased, accents and punctuation removed, spaces collapsed, the statement's own words (achat, crédit, débit TWINT, paiement, ordre permanent, paiement de salaire) and a processor prefix ("PayUp *", "XYZ*") dropped. A rule holds a fragment and a category and matches a key that contains it; the longest matching fragment wins; a rule whose category is not in force on a row's date does not apply to it. The one-click offer proposes the transaction's whole key; Settings can shorten it. A category's first subcategory moves its rules to Other; deleting a category deletes its rules.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-057: one implementation of the key, robust to the bank's cut names, capitals and processor prefixes (docs/import-sources.md).
rejected: Exact match on the description: rarely matches again.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Uncategorised imports go to a "to categorise" category
decisions.decision: Each budget gets, at its first import that needs it, one ordinary top-level category flagged as its "to categorise" place (the name the caller passes; from the first period; created even at the 200 / 500 category limits, within the 900-row bound). Rows without a member's category or an applying rule land there. It is renamable, has no expectation, takes no subcategory, cannot end while it holds transactions, and a transaction in it cannot be confirmed.
decisions.why: Every expense and refund keeps a category, so totals, progress and comparison keep adding up; the review has one place to empty.
rejected: A null category for imported rows: breaks every per-category sum.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Duplicates are counted
decisions.decision: Rows of one import are never duplicates of each other. A row is compared with every existing transaction of the same kind, whatever its origin: the same bank transaction id, else the same date, amount and description. Each existing transaction absorbs at most one row, so the same statement imported twice imports nothing the second time. Import anyway is per row or for all skipped rows of a batch.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-056 (coordinator decision).
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Flagged entries and remembered choices
decisions.decision: Card-bill payments and own transfers (from the source's hint) are skipped by default; a transfer to another person, also of the household, is an ordinary expense unless skipped. A member's choice for a flagged row (import or skip) is remembered per budget (not per member), per kind of flag and counterparty key, and proposed next time; a token's import remembers nothing.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-063 and Q-064 (coordinator decision).
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Reconciliation by possible match
decisions.decision: A row is a possible match of an existing transaction of the same kind that was not imported (typed, or a charge), with the same amount and a date within three days. Default: skip the row; when the match is a charge awaiting confirmation, the import confirms it and the preview says so; the member can import the row anyway. Each existing transaction absorbs one row. With a token, matches are skipped and left for the member.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-068 (coordinator decision).
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Import tokens
decisions.decision: A member creates a token for one budget with a name and an expiry (30 days by default, at most a year); the secret (bti_ and 244 random bits) is answered once and only its SHA-256 is stored. At most 10 active and 100 tokens a budget. import_with_token is the only function callable without a session: an unknown, expired or revoked token gets invalid_token after one index lookup, before any lock or catch-up. A token imports with the default choices only, never confirms a charge, remembers nothing, and its answer is counts and the reasons of rows refused for their own content (budget-dependent outcomes are not told). Per token: 60 calls and 5000 rows an hour, 300 calls and 20 000 rows a day. Revoking takes the budget lock; a member leaving (or removed, or deleted) revokes the tokens they created.
decisions.why: D-116 and R-SECURITY-005: a token can only add, cannot read, and a stolen one does bounded, reviewable harm.
rejected: Telling the token which rows were duplicates: an oracle on the budget's transactions.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: A salary credit
decisions.decision: A credit is a salary credit when the source says so (hint salary) or when its amount equals the amount of an income in force in the period of its date and its date is within five days of that period's start. It is skipped by default; imported anyway it is extra income. A different amount than the planned income changes nothing by itself; the preview shows the planned amount beside the row's.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-065 (coordinator decision).
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: A credit reviewed as a refund
decisions.decision: A credit is a refund by default (in the category a rule or the member gives, else "to categorise"), counted in the period of its date, and may take the category's spending below zero; the member may make it extra income instead.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-066 (coordinator decision).
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: What a batch records
decisions.decision: A batch records its source kind, the statement's date range, its counts (rows, imported, duplicates, flagged, matches, skipped by choice, invalid, charges confirmed), who imported (the member, or the token and its name) and when; never a file name, an account or a card number. Its skipped rows are kept, with why, for the member.
decisions.why: Q-070 stays open for accounts (step 7); the review needs to know what each import did.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Undoing an import batch
decisions.decision: A member can undo a batch once: its transactions still to review are deleted, the confirmed ones stay, charges it confirmed stay confirmed, remembered choices stay; the answer says how many of each. An undone batch takes no more chunks.
decisions.why: Coordinator decision; a wrong import is removed without touching what was already reviewed.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Choices of the database developer for the import
decisions.decision: Beyond the coordinator's defaults: a credit defaults to a refund (not extra income); hint transfer_to_person names a transfer to another person (imported by default, its choice remembered); details may also carry location; a row with an unknown key is refused; a token's answer counts rows refused for the budget's sake as received; "import anyway" drops a row's original kind and category (the review decides); the "to categorise" category is created even at the category limits.
decisions.why: Each keeps the token free of reads and the review in one place; the rest follow the sources (docs/import-sources.md).
source: owner-request: database developer decision for step 6, within the coordinator's brief, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Accounts
decisions.decision: An account has a name, a kind (current or salary, savings, third pillar, tax reserve, investment, cash, credit card, other), an optional bank label and an optional member it belongs to (none: shared). It counts from a period and can be closed from a period, like a category; earlier periods keep it. Its name, kind, label and holder are not versioned: a rename shows everywhere, past periods included. It keeps its holder after the member leaves (shown as a former member); an account whose holder deleted their login becomes shared. No balance (D-123).
decisions.why: The coordinator's defaults for step 7; renames read like categories'. Closing an account a member held when they leave would break the transfers of the others.
rejected: Versioning the name or the kind.
Closing a member's accounts when they leave.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 7 database (accounts and money flow), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The account an income is paid into
decisions.decision: An income can name the account it is paid into: part of its terms (optional), versioned with them, changed from the current period or as a correction like an amount. An income with no account flows into one "not assigned" node of the money flow, so its totals still add up.
decisions.why: The flow starts where the salary arrives, which changes when a member changes bank.
rejected: A field of the income itself, the same in every period.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 7 database (accounts and money flow), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Schedules and due dates of planned transfers
decisions.decision: A transfer has exactly one occurrence in each period it is in force. On a fixed day of the month (1 to 31): the first date with that day on or after the period's start, clamped to the month's length, no weekend rule. From a pay date: the chosen income's actual pay date in the period plus 0 to 31 days (never negative); the primary income's actual pay date in a period is the period's start (an early salary and a moved boundary included); another income's is its first actual pay date on or after the period's start, under its terms then. Where the chosen income is not in force (ended, its member gone), the transfer follows the primary income, and the checklist and overview say so. A due date is never after the period's last day. Answers Q-059.
decisions.why: The coordinator's defaults. A period starts on the primary salary, so its start is that salary's actual date, whatever moved it; this needs no other record of past pay dates.
rejected: A weekend rule for fixed days.
Negative offsets.
Several occurrences per period, or none.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 7 database (accounts and money flow), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Transactions of transfers linked to a category
decisions.decision: An automatic transfer is assumed done on its due date, without confirmation (only subscription charges are confirmed). Linked to a category, its transaction is created by the catch-up on its due date: dated then, at the planned amount of its period, confirmed, exactly once, held back at the transaction limit; marked not done, its transaction is deleted and not created again; undoing that creates it again. A manual transfer linked to a category gets its transaction when marked done, dated the done date, with the amount moved (default the planned amount); undoing "done" deletes it. Deleting the transaction puts the occurrence back (a manual one to do, an automatic one not done). Editing its amount or date is allowed and shows on the occurrence. Answers Q-060.
decisions.why: The coordinator's defaults: recorded once (D-122), and the transaction exists exactly when the transfer counts as done.
rejected: Automatic transfers awaiting confirmation like subscription charges.
Undoing "done" keeping the transaction.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 7 database (accounts and money flow), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Occurrences are computed, marks are stored
decisions.decision: An occurrence is computed from the transfer's terms in force in a period and that period's boundaries; only what was done is stored: one mark at most per transfer and period (done, skipped, not done), the catch-up's included. The catch-up settles each transfer's periods in order (transfers.settled_seq) within its bounded step, after the subscription charges. An edit or a correction of the terms settles again the periods it governs, so an automatic linked occurrence already due without a mark gets its transaction then, past periods of a correction included.
decisions.why: Past occurrences follow the plan as corrected without rows to rewrite; settling again after an edit keeps "a transaction exists exactly when an automatic linked transfer counts as done" true for every period.
rejected: A row per transfer and period.
Never creating a transaction for a period already passed after a correction, as for subscription charges (Q-221).
source: owner-request: database developer decision for step 7, within the coordinator's brief, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Nothing deletes a transfer's transaction implicitly
decisions.decision: Only a member's act deletes a transfer's transaction: undoing "done", marking an automatic transfer not done, or deleting the transaction. Ending a transfer, closing what it uses, or a member leaving keeps it: when its mark goes, the transaction stays as an ordinary one. The one exception is a reopen (D-358).
decisions.why: A transaction is money the member sees in the totals; it never disappears behind an edit of the plan.
rejected: Deleting the catch-up's transactions when a transfer ends from their period.
source: owner-request: database developer decision for step 7, within the coordinator's brief, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The money flow read
decisions.decision: One call, get_money_flow, typed rows (income, not_assigned, account, transfer, total), from the plan in force in the chosen period (default the current one), never from transactions: incomes at their amounts then (salaries only: their total is period_summaries.salary_total; extra incomes are actual transactions, not plan), transfers at their planned amounts, every account in force with what comes in, what goes out and what stays (in minus out, flagged when negative). No balance.
decisions.why: The coordinator's defaults; a diagram of the plan stays the same whatever was spent.
rejected: Extra incomes in the flow.
Reading actual transfers.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 7 database (accounts and money flow), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Limits of accounts and transfers
decisions.decision: 50 accounts and 50 planned transfers in force, 200 of each in all (void ones not counted), 900 rows of each a budget (R-APP-170); previews list at most 60 occurrences; an offset is at most 31 days; a bank label at most 100 characters.
decisions.why: Like subscriptions and debts; every read stays within the API's 1000 rows.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 7 database (accounts and money flow), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Reopen and the marks of the merged period
decisions.decision: A mark of the merged period moves to the reopened period when that period has none for the transfer. Otherwise it goes: one made by the catch-up with its transaction (made again if the period comes back, like a debt's interest), a member's leaving its transaction as an ordinary one. A transfer ended in the merged period ends in the reopened one, and its marks there go the same way. Every transfer is settled again from the reopened period.
decisions.why: The reopened period keeps what happened in it; the catch-up's assumption of the merged period would otherwise be counted twice once the period comes back.
rejected: Keeping the catch-up's transaction as an ordinary one (counted twice later).
source: owner-request: database developer decision for step 7, within the coordinator's brief, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Transfers in the committed amounts
decisions.decision: A linked transfer's planned amount is committed in its category in each period it is in force, as its own figure: transfer_committed in get_period_progress, transfer_committed_amount in category_overview, transfer_committed_total in period_summaries; never added to the subscriptions' committed amount, so every existing figure is unchanged.
decisions.why: The coordinator's default ("yes, as its own kind"); keeping it apart avoids changing what committed meant.
rejected: Adding it to committed.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 7 database (accounts and money flow), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Marks of an occurrence
decisions.decision: A mark is made from no mark (revision 0) and undone back to none; changing a mark means undoing it first. Only a manual transfer is marked done or skipped, only an automatic one not done. Done's date defaults to today in the current period, else to the due date, and is never after today. Every mark and undo names the revision of the mark the member read.
decisions.why: One state per occurrence and one way between states keep two members' marks from crossing (R-CONCURRENCY-230).
rejected: Changing a mark in place.
source: owner-request: database developer decision for step 7, within the coordinator's brief, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The dashboard counts of manual transfers
decisions.decision: my_budgets.transfers_to_do and transfers_overdue count the current period's manual transfers still to do and, of those, the ones whose due date has passed; past periods' unfinished ones show in their own checklist only.
decisions.why: A bounded read on every page; a forgotten transfer of an earlier period is rare and visible in that period.
rejected: Counting every past period (unbounded over the budget's life).
source: owner-request: database developer decision for step 7, within the coordinator's brief, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Import tokens (revised)
decisions.decision: A member creates a token for one budget with a name and an expiry (30 days by default, at most a year); the secret (bti_ and 244 random bits) is answered once and only its SHA-256 is stored. At most 10 tokens that can still be used a budget; a revoked or expired one can be deleted, and those kept are pruned to the newest 20 and 365 days. import_with_token is the only function callable without a session, by POST only (a GET is refused with read_only_call before the token is looked at). An unknown, expired or revoked token, or one whose creator left, was removed or deleted their account, gets invalid_token after one index lookup, before any lock or catch-up. A call never waits for another token call: the same token busy, or every slot for token work taken, answers token_busy or imports_busy at once, doing nothing and counting nothing (D-453). Every call that does work counts, whatever its outcome, cancelled included: 60 calls and 5000 rows within any 60 minutes, 300 calls and 20 000 rows within any 24 hours (by whole minutes: a call counts 60 to 61 minutes and 24 hours to 24 hours and 1 minute, D-463), checked and counted in one step under the token's lock; a refusal after the count is answered in the error column, not raised. A token call takes at most 250 rows. The batch records the token, never the caller. Batches, skipped rows and remembered choices are read through paged functions only.
decisions.why: The step 6 review: a refused call must cost the attacker too, parallel calls must not pass the limit together, fixed hourly windows let twice the limit through at the boundary, tokens must not pile up, and a token in a URL ends up in logs.
rejected: Counting only successful calls: free probing.
Fixed clock-hour windows.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: What a token is told
decisions.decision: A token's answer does not depend on the budget's content: every argument is checked before anything of the budget, "to categorise" is created under its fixed name (the token cannot name it), and a token is never told how many rows would fit. Coarse states still reach it, because a script must be able to say why nothing was imported: the budget is nearly full (transaction_limit_reached, refused whenever it has room for fewer than 250 transactions, D-451), the budget is far behind (catching_up), its import storage of the day is used up (import_limit_reached, D-452), and its lock was held for more than a second (budget_busy, D-453).
decisions.why: Answer to Q-191 and the step 6 review (F1): any budget-dependent difference is an oracle on the budget's transactions.
rejected: Hiding the two coarse states: the script could not explain a refusal.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Duplicates are counted per batch
decisions.decision: Rows of one batch are never duplicates of each other. A row is compared with every existing transaction of the same kind, whatever its origin: the same bank transaction id, else the same date, amount and description, either as the transaction is now or as it was first imported. Each existing transaction absorbs at most one row of the batch, counted over all its chunks, whatever order they arrive in and however often one is sent again; the same statement imported twice imports nothing the second time. Import anyway is per row or for all skipped rows of a batch.
decisions.why: The step 6 review (F4, F17): counting per chunk let a statement split in two chunks import a duplicate, and editing an imported transaction made the same line import again.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Possible matches: nearest date, once per batch
decisions.decision: A row is a possible match of an existing transaction of the same kind that was not imported (typed, or a charge), with the same amount and a date within three days either way; descriptions are not compared. Each existing transaction goes to the row nearest in date (ties: the earlier row, then a charge awaiting confirmation) and absorbs at most one row of the batch. Default: skip the row; when the match is a charge awaiting confirmation the import confirms it and the preview says so; the member can import the row anyway. The batch counts its matched rows. With a token, matches are skipped and left for the member.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-192: bank descriptions rarely look like what a member typed, so comparing them would miss most matches; the nearest date is the likeliest pair.
rejected: Matching only when the descriptions look alike.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Confirming a frozen import
decisions.decision: Confirming an imported transaction changes no amount, date, category or link, so it is allowed on a frozen transaction (a payment of an ended debt).
decisions.why: Undo keeps frozen transactions (D-379); the member must still be able to empty the review.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: "To categorise" is the import's place only
decisions.decision: Each budget gets, at its first import that needs it, one top-level category flagged as its "to categorise" place (the name the member passes, a fixed name for a token; from the first period; created even at the category limits). Only imported transactions still to review can be in it: no hand-typed transaction, subscription, debt, planned transfer or merchant rule uses it, and it does not count toward the 200 categories in force. It is renamable, has no expectation, takes no subcategory, cannot end while it holds transactions, and a transaction in it cannot be confirmed. my_budgets names it only while it is in force; category_overview flags it.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-190 and the step 6 review (F12): it is a waiting room, not a category to plan with.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: One cleaner for free text
decisions.decision: Every name and description of every step goes through one helper: control characters and bidirectional or zero-width formatting characters are removed, every other run of white space becomes one space, and the result is trimmed, before validation and before any comparison. An import's details are stored normalised the same way. Markup and spreadsheet formulas stay as text: the screens escape them, and an export must neutralise them.
decisions.why: The step 6 review (F13): the same text must compare equal wherever it came from, and invisible characters must not hide what a name says.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: A salary credit (revised)
decisions.decision: A credit is a salary credit when the source says so (hint salary) or when its amount equals an income's amount and its date is within five days either side of a period start: on or after the start of its own period, or before the start of the next period (projected when it does not exist yet), at the income's amount in force in that period. It is skipped by default; imported anyway it is extra income. A different amount changes nothing by itself; the preview shows the planned amount beside the row's.
decisions.why: The step 6 review (F9): a salary paid a few days before the period it starts was missed.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Refused rows are stored bounded
decisions.decision: Of a row that was not imported, only its known keys are kept, each within its limit, and only the names of unknown keys; a call whose rows argument exceeds 2 MB is refused whole (invalid_rows) before any row is read; the request body itself is read and parsed before the function runs, so what bounds it there is the gateway (not verified for the hosted project: Q-280).
decisions.why: The step 6 review (F3): a stolen token could otherwise store megabytes of arbitrary JSON per call.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Undo and rules leave linked and frozen transactions alone
decisions.decision: Undoing a batch deletes only its transactions still to review that are linked to nothing; one linked to a subscription, a debt or a planned transfer stays (it is frozen or belongs to that record) and is counted as kept_linked, the confirmed ones as kept_confirmed. Applying a merchant rule at once moves only transactions to review in "to categorise" that are linked to nothing. Every bulk write of steps 6 and 7 was checked against the freeze rules.
decisions.why: The step 6 review (F5): undo deleted a frozen debt payment and a rule moved a linked charge.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Ending a transfer keeps what was done
decisions.decision: Only a member's act deletes a transfer's transaction: undoing "done", marking an automatic transfer not done, or deleting the transaction. Ending a transfer removes its occurrences from that period on but keeps every mark already made and every transaction link; a period's checklist lists the transfers in force plus those with a mark or a transaction there, flagged as ended (is_ended); preview_end_transfer answers only the outcome or the refusal. The one exception is a reopen (D-382).
decisions.why: The step 6 review's step 7 change: what a member recorded is history; ending the plan must not rewrite it.
rejected: Removing the marks from the end on (the step 7 version).
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database, step 7 change, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The merchant key's cases
decisions.decision: The key is the merchant field when it has a letter or digit, else the description; lower case, accents removed (ß, œ, æ, ø spelled out), any script kept; the statement's leading words dropped and a '*' resolved repeatedly: a processor before the merchant ("payup *shop" is "shop"), a merchant before a reference ("amazon.de*ab12cd" is "amazon.de"). The key of a key is itself.
decisions.why: The step 6 review: the listed cases gave keys that no rule could match.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Reopen and the marks of the merged period (revised)
decisions.decision: A mark of the merged period moves to the reopened period when that period has none for the transfer. Otherwise it goes: one made by the catch-up with its transaction (made again if the period comes back, like a debt's interest), a member's leaving its transaction as an ordinary one. Marks of periods where a transfer is no longer in force after the merge stay, like any mark of an ended transfer (D-380). Every transfer is settled again from the reopened period.
decisions.why: D-380: an ended transfer keeps its marks; the reopen follows the same rule.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database, step 7 change, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Averages over the completed periods, and a category's own average
decisions.decision: An average is the sum over the completed periods of the range divided by their number, rounded to the rappen with halves away from zero (also for a negative result); null when none is completed. The average result is the average of the results, so it can differ by a rappen from the average income minus the average spent. A category's average spent divides by every completed period of the range (so the categories' averages add up to the trend's); beside it, active_average_spent divides by active_count, the completed periods of the range in which the category was in force or had spending (null when that count is 0), for a category that started or stopped inside the range.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-160 (coordinator decision): Daycare, CHF 800 in each of its 3 periods of 11, showed an average of 218.18.
rejected: Replacing the average over the whole range: the lines would no longer add up to the trend.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 5 database and the step 4 re-review fixes, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The comparison's default and its running periods
decisions.decision: With no period given, get_period_comparison compares the last two completed periods when two exist, otherwise the last two periods (B the current period, or the last once the budget has ended). With only A given, B is the current (or last) period; with only B given, A is the one before. Every row says, per side, whether it is the current period (a_is_current, b_is_current) and whether it is completed (a_is_completed, b_is_completed; null for a missing side A).
decisions.why: Answer to Q-161 (coordinator decision): on day 4 of the running period the default showed a difference of -1606.00, which read as a large saving.
rejected: Keeping the current period as the default B.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 5 database and the step 4 re-review fixes, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Memberships and invitations are bounded
decisions.decision: A user belongs to at most 50 budgets, owned ones included (owned stays at 20): accepting an invitation or creating a budget beyond that answers membership_limit_reached; both are serialised per user. list_my_invitations is paged: oldest first, p_limit 1 to 200 (default 50), next page after the last row's created_at and id.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-162 (coordinator decision): my_budgets took 3.5 s for 1000 rows and would be cut silently; 1020 pending invitations came back as 1000.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 5 database and the step 4 re-review fixes, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Interest and moved boundaries (revised)
decisions.decision: D-272 holds as a statement about the stored data after any change of a period's boundaries: a period's interest entry exists only for a debt opened before the period's start. A start may not move to on or before the opening of a debt that has an interest entry in that period: the change is refused with interest_before_opening and nothing is removed (D-467; a trigger on the period's start, so every boundary operation is covered); preview_move_period_start gives that refusal, and its interest_removed is always 0. The other way, a start moved later so that a debt is now opened before the start of a period without an entry, adds nothing: interest is computed once, when the period is created, on the balance before its start, and computing it afterwards would charge a period that began, as recorded, before the debt existed, on a balance that already includes later rows.
decisions.why: The step 5 review (M1): a moved start put a period's interest before the debt's opening, so the history began with interest.
rejected: Adding the interest when a start moves later: a retroactive charge on a balance that is no longer the one before the start.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 5 database and the step 4 re-review fixes, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Far behind, only the catch-up calls work
decisions.decision: A call other than ensure_periods and get_current_period answers catching_up at once, before the budget lock and without any work, when the budget's last period ended more than 62 days before today (or its end date); within that it does its own roll-over as before. Only ensure_periods and get_current_period (and create_budget, for its first periods) do multi-period work, one step per call (at most 120 periods and about two seconds), however often the catch-up is called within one statement. They wait at most two seconds for a lock another session holds, then answer catching_up, so the client's loop tries again and never meets the statement timeout. Supersedes D-270 (whose bound and step stay).
decisions.why: The step 5 review (S1, S5): a refused call did a whole step under the lock and discarded it, so six calls at once ran into the 8 s timeout, ensure_periods included; clearing the end date of a long-ended budget did two steps in one call.
rejected: Every call doing a step and discarding it (the D-270 behaviour).
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 5 database and the step 4 re-review fixes, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: A held charge in the schedule preview
decisions.decision: preview_update_subscription refuses with charge_held_back where update_subscription would (a new cadence or next charge date while a charge is held), and its schedule starts with the held date, the next charge date subscription_overview shows.
decisions.why: The step 5 review (S4): the preview answered dates the write then refused, and started a month late.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 5 database and the step 4 re-review fixes, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The overviews compute only what can differ
decisions.decision: category_overview computes the per-row helpers only where their answer can differ: a category not in force now (ended, void) has no committed amount, no transfer committed amount and is in no use (terms may only use a category in force, R-CATEGORY-130), and one that started before now never deletes on removal (its references are not looked up).
decisions.why: The step 5 review (S8): at the 900-row cap, committed_amount, removal_deletes and in_use cost most of category_overview's 1.2 to 1.6 s.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 5 database and the step 4 re-review fixes, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: A retried add records once
decisions.decision: add_transaction, add_income, create_category, create_subscription, create_debt, create_account and create_transfer take an optional p_client_id (a uuid the client generates once per user action and sends with every retry). The first call records the id with the ids of the rows it created (kept 7 days); the same id sent again by the same member, for the same budget, the same call and the same arguments, creates nothing and answers those rows as they are now (none if deleted since). The same id from another member, for another budget, another call or other arguments is refused with request_reused before anything is written, and the refusal says nothing about the first request. The check runs under the budget lock, so a double click waits for the first call and answers its rows. Retries of the other writes are already harmless: edits, ends, marks (mark_transfer_done) and balance adjustments (adjust_debt_balance) name the revision they read and answer record_changed on a retry; an import chunk is idempotent by batch and chunk.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-090 (coordinator decision): a lost answer made the screen say nothing was saved, the user saved again, and the transaction was recorded twice.
rejected: Overwriting or returning another member's record for a reused id.
source: owner-request: coordinator, screen review of steps 4 and 5, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Over the plan, from the progress view
decisions.decision: get_category_trend has is_overspent (boolean[], aligned with period_ids): get_period_progress's is_overspent of the line in each period, false where the line has no progress row. get_period_comparison's category rows have a_is_overspent and b_is_overspent, the progress view's flag of each side (null where the side has no row, and on the total row). The client never decides it from spent and planned.
decisions.why: The screen review: the Compare page decided spent > planned in the client, which differs from the progress view for a category not in force with spending (C-LOGIC-003).
source: owner-request: coordinator, screen review of steps 4 and 5, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The budget's first and last day in my_budgets
decisions.decision: my_budgets.first_period_start is the first period's start, the earliest date the budget accepts a transaction; my_budgets.end_date (already there) is the ended budget's last day (the end of the period containing the end date entered, projected while it does not exist).
decisions.why: The screen review: beyond 120 periods the transaction form only had the first page of list_periods.
source: owner-request: coordinator, screen review of steps 4 and 5, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Removing a mark looks at the occurrence again
decisions.decision: Every removal of a transfer's mark (undoing it, deleting the transaction of a manual one) moves the transfer's watermark (settled_seq) back before that period, so the catch-up looks at the occurrence again; undoing a mark of an automatic linked occurrence that is due creates its transaction within the same call. Deleting the transaction of a done occurrence follows the terms in force for it now: an automatic transfer is then not done (its transaction is never created again), whoever marked it; a manual one is to do again.
decisions.why: The step 7 review (M1): the watermark stayed past a period whose mark was removed, so an automatic linked occurrence showed done, held back, with no transaction, for good.
source: owner-request: coordinator, independent review of the step 7 database (79afb45), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The dashboard counts the period before too
decisions.decision: transfers_to_do and transfers_overdue (get_transfers_to_do, a read of its own since D-494) count the manual occurrences still to do of the current period and of the period before it.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-222 (coordinator decision): a transfer left undone at the end of a period must not vanish from the dashboard the day the salary arrives.
source: owner-request: coordinator, independent review of the step 7 database (79afb45), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: A kept income is not checked as newly chosen
decisions.decision: An edit of a pay-date transfer validates only an income it chooses (p_income_id): the income kept from the terms before may have ended, and the transfer then follows the primary income (follows_primary), as it already did.
decisions.why: The step 7 review: once the chosen income had ended, every edit and the preview with no argument answered income_not_in_force until the client cleared the income.
source: owner-request: coordinator, independent review of the step 7 database (79afb45), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: No end while a transaction is held back
decisions.decision: Ending a transfer from a period is refused with transfer_held_back while an automatic linked occurrence from that period on is due and waits for room (the budget holds the most transactions): ending would drop it for good. Free room first, as for a subscription's held charge (charge_held_back). preview_end_transfer gives it as the refusal.
decisions.why: The step 7 review: in a full budget, ending from the current period dropped that period's held occurrence.
source: owner-request: coordinator, independent review of the step 7 database (79afb45), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The previews say what is created at once, counted
decisions.decision: preview_create_transfer and preview_update_transfer mark created_at_once only where the budget has room (in order), and give on every row created_at_once_count: how many transactions the write creates at once over every period it governs, beyond the at most p_count rows listed.
decisions.why: The step 7 review: created_at_once was true in a full budget where nothing is created, and a correction over 63 periods created 63 while the preview listed 60.
source: owner-request: coordinator, independent review of the step 7 database (79afb45), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The comparison carries the transfers' committed figure
decisions.decision: get_period_trend has transfer_committed_total, get_category_trend transfer_committed (bigint[] aligned with period_ids, the progress view's figure of the line), and get_period_comparison a_transfer_committed, b_transfer_committed and transfer_committed_difference (total row: the periods' totals; category rows: the progress view's figure), apart from the subscriptions' committed figures.
decisions.why: The step 7 review: the comparison reads showed the subscriptions' committed amounts only.
source: owner-request: coordinator, independent review of the step 7 database (79afb45), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The history table newest first, the chart oldest first
decisions.decision: The debt page reads get_debt_history twice: the table newest first (p_newest_first) 50 rows a page, older ones on request; the chart oldest first, 1000 rows a page, up to 10 000 events, saying where it stops.
decisions.why: The database now pages newest first (answer to Q-141): the latest events, the ones a member looks for, come first; D-232's reason for oldest first no longer holds.
source: owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens adapted to the database re-review and step 5, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: catching_up is handled in one place
decisions.decision: One component watches every query and mutation of the budget for catching_up: it runs ensure_periods until 0 behind the catching-up screen (shown only after 700 ms), then reads the budget's queries again. Pages stay mounted, so forms keep what was typed; a refused save says to save again.
decisions.why: Since D-270 every call but ensure_periods and get_current_period answers catching_up when the budget is behind; handling it per screen would miss some, and remounting pages would lose what was typed. A catch-up of one step (a new day) ends in about 100 ms: a flash of the full screen helps nobody.
rejected: Remounting the page after the catch-up: loses form content.
source: owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens adapted to the database re-review and step 5, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Older periods are read on request, from every picker
decisions.decision: usePeriods reads list_periods 120 at a time; the periods page has a button for older periods, and every period picker ends with "Older periods…", which reads the next page (the list stays open for the next choice).
decisions.why: R-APP-170: a budget's periods grow without bound and the API cuts an answer at 1000 rows. Ten years fit in one page, so the entry is rarely seen.
rejected: Loading every page at once: what the paging is for.
source: owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens adapted to the database re-review and step 5, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Frozen payments from the list itself
decisions.decision: The transactions list and form read transaction_list.debt_ended to know that a payment's debt has ended; they no longer read debt_overview for it.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-140: the database gives the flag on the row.
source: owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens adapted to the database re-review and step 5, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Typed values survive a change of correction period
decisions.decision: When the user picks another correction period, the fields they changed keep what they typed; the others take the new period's terms (the rule of "Keep mine").
decisions.why: Replacing typed values without notice loses work; saying what was replaced is noisier than keeping it.
rejected: Saying what was replaced and replacing it anyway.
source: owner-request: coordinator, final review of the step 4 screens (addendum C), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Compare is a page of its own after the dashboard
decisions.decision: The comparison is a sidebar page placed right after the dashboard, with three views reached by links whose choices live in the address; Recharts is loaded only with this page. No dashboard card for step 5.
decisions.why: The comparison is read often and for a while; a page of its own keeps the dashboard light and its first load small, and the address makes a view shareable between members.
rejected: Tabs inside the periods or progress page.
A dashboard card with a small trend (optional in the brief; left out for now).
source: owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens adapted to the database re-review and step 5, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Say lengths differ beyond a tenth
decisions.decision: The trend says that period lengths differ and amounts are not adjusted only when the longest period of the range is more than 1.1 times the shortest (from the days the database gives); periods of 28 to 31 days do not trigger it.
decisions.why: The note matters after an early pay date or a reopened period; under every ordinary range it would be noise.
rejected: Always showing the note.
Amounts per day (R-COMPARE-173 forbids scaling).
source: owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens adapted to the database re-review and step 5, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Chart forms of the comparison
decisions.decision: Income and spending as columns side by side with the planned total as a line on one money axis; the result in a chart of its own, columns from zero (position tells a surplus from a deficit); category lines as a line chart of at most five user-picked lines, each in the hue of its slot. Every chart is one named image whose text alternative is the table under it; on a phone a wide range scrolls inside the chart's own frame, opening on the newest periods.
decisions.why: One scale per chart; a slot keeps its colour so identity never moves with rank; five hues is what stays distinguishable.
rejected: Two y-axes on one chart.
Stacked areas of every category.
A chart of every line.
source: owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens adapted to the database re-review and step 5, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Side by side on a phone
decisions.decision: Below the small breakpoint each row of the side-by-side tables shows its name, then A and B next to each other, then the difference on a line of its own, each figure labelled; wider screens keep the table.
decisions.why: The difference is what the view is for: it must be seen without scrolling sideways, also with eight-figure amounts at 320 px.
rejected: A table scrolling sideways on phones.
source: owner-request: coordinator, step 4 screens adapted to the database re-review and step 5, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Rounded figures are checked within 0.05
decisions.decision: Where a statement prints a product it rounds (an amount times an exchange rate, a processing fee as a percentage, a CHF amount charged abroad plus its fee), the parser accepts the printed figure when it differs from the exact product by less than CHF 0.05; a securities quantity times its price must give the amount within one unit of the quantity's last decimal times the price, plus one rappen. Every sum, subtotal, carried-forward line, total and running balance must match exactly.
decisions.why: R-IMPORT-088 asks for the arithmetic the statement prints to be checked, but the banks' rounding rules are not known (Q-205): every CHF figure of the card-bill sample is a multiple of 0.05, and one row differs from its printed parts by 0.02. A bound below 0.05 accepts any rounding to 0.05 (nearest, up or down) and still refuses a misread digit.
rejected: Requiring exact products, which refuses real statements.
Not checking rates and fees, which lets a misread rate through.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Unknown entry types are kept, malformed known ones refused
decisions.decision: Inside a statement the parser recognises, an entry of a type it does not know (a cash withdrawal, an interest or fee line, a Yuh sale ...) is kept with its printed text as description and the default of its direction; a hint is added only from a leading label (Retrait, Intérêt, Frais ...). An entry that starts like a known type (Achat, Débit TWINT, Paiement, a Yuh Achat with security lines) but does not match its pattern refuses the statement, as does any item outside the table's columns or any amount the parser cannot explain.
decisions.why: The samples show few entry types; refusing every statement with a new type would make the import useless, while the column totals and balances still prove that every unknown entry has the right amount (R-IMPORT-088). A known type that does not match is a sign the layout changed.
rejected: Refusing a statement with any unknown entry type.
Skipping lines the parser does not understand.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: pdf.js loaded on demand, fetching nothing
decisions.decision: Statements are read with pdfjs-dist 6.4.299, the version the fixtures were captured with, imported dynamically on the first read so that the main bundle does not grow. Its worker is a same-origin file emitted by the build (production CSP: script-src 'self', worker-src 'self' blob:). No CMap, standard font, ICC profile or wasm decoder is configured or fetched (fetching in the worker and wasm are off), fonts are not installed into the page, and the bytes are passed in memory. Files above 10 MB or 50 pages are refused before or right after opening.
decisions.why: D-127 keeps the file in the browser; fetching resources from a CDN would leak that a statement is being read and break the CSP. Bank statements embed their fonts and need none of these resources for their text. Monthly statements are a few pages and well under 1 MB, so the bounds leave a wide margin while stopping a hostile file early.
rejected: Bundling pdf.js in the main chunk.
Loading the worker or resources from a CDN.
A newer pdf.js than the fixtures were captured with.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Parsers return codes and data; the screens own the words
decisions.decision: A parse returns the recognised source, what identifies the statement (its period or bill date), one entry per transaction with codes (direction, hint, proposed handling) and the extra data, the controls it checked, and the full source-specific document in the shape of the fixtures' expected.json. A refusal is a typed reason with its figures (the control, the printed and computed amounts) or the line it could not read. The English notes of expected.json (handling.why, skipped.reason) are kept for the fixture comparison as developer notes; the screens translate the codes, never these notes.
decisions.why: The screens are bilingual (R-I18N) and R-IMPORT-100 compares the parse with expected.json exactly.
rejected: Returning user-facing messages from the parsers.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: An own transfer needs the holder's name and address
decisions.decision: A payment or standing order on the Migros Bank account, and a transfer received on Yuh, is flagged as a transfer between the owner's own accounts when the counterparty's name has the same words as the holder's name (in either order) and its street and town lines equal the holder's address, compared without case, punctuation or spacing (Yuh prints "Chemin du Test, 12"). The country line and the IBAN are not compared.
decisions.why: docs/import-sources.md names the name and the address as the only clues on the Migros Bank statement, and says a payment to another person at the same address is not an own transfer (Q-063). Applying the same test to Yuh keeps one rule for both and flags the sample's transfer.
rejected: The name alone, which would flag a namesake.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Any credit before the first card is the payment received
decisions.decision: On a card bill, a dated row with a trailing minus before the first card section is the payment received, whatever its label ("Votre paiement - Merci", with LSV, partial, upper case or another wording), and is skipped like it. A debit row there must be the late-payment interest or a fee, or the bill is refused.
decisions.why: Review: under any other label the payment came out as a credit to review while the bill still added up, so no control fired and the card-bill payment would have been counted twice. Matching the position and the sign, not the words, holds for every wording.
rejected: Matching the label "Votre paiement - Merci" only.
source: owner-request: coordinator, review round of the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: A repeated bank id identifies no transaction
decisions.decision: A bank transaction id (TWINT id, Yuh reference) printed on more than one entry of the same statement is not a transaction id: every entry carrying it gets none, and all the entries stay. This also answers whether a TWINT id can repeat: the parser does not assume it cannot.
decisions.why: With "same bank id means duplicate", a repeated id (a reversal, a split booking, a misprint) would lose a transaction; an entry without an id is still imported. Identical genuine entries with different ids keep their ids.
rejected: Keeping the id on the first entry only.
Refusing the statement.
source: owner-request: coordinator, review round of the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Unknown entries described by their first line; text outside tables ignored
decisions.decision: Inside a statement the parser recognises, an entry of a type it does not know is kept, described by its first text line only (the other lines, which can name people, addresses or IBANs, stay in textLines on the device), with the default of its direction; a hint comes only from a leading label (Retrait, Intérêt, Frais ...) or from the statement's own category line, never from a word inside a merchant name. An entry that starts like a known type but does not match its pattern or its column, any item outside the table's columns, and a rotated or right-to-left item inside a table refuse the statement. Text outside the tables is ignored: page headers and footers, the lines after "Montant dû" on the card bill, and Yuh lines outside a currency table.
decisions.why: Supersedes D-331, whose wording ("any item outside the table's columns refuses") did not say that rotated items were dropped and text outside the tables ignored, and whose descriptions of unknown entries could carry a third party's address and IBAN.
rejected: Refusing a statement with any unknown entry type.
Skipping lines the parser does not understand.
The whole entry text as description.
source: owner-request: coordinator, review round of the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Bounds on items, page size and time
decisions.decision: Each read has its own pdf.js worker, stopped when the read ends. A page outside 500 to 700 by 700 to 1000 pt is refused before its text is read; the text is streamed and the read stops beyond 5000 items on a page or 20 000 in the document; after 20 seconds the worker is terminated and the file refused. Lines are grouped in one pass over the items sorted by baseline. The same item and page bounds apply to a text layer given directly to the parser. A reader that cannot be loaded (offline, a release replaced its chunk) is a refusal of its own, and any other fault while reading a refusal too: the entry point never throws.
decisions.why: Review: a 425 kB PDF with one very tall page and 120 000 lines stalled the main thread for 53 s, and a 916 kB PDF inflating to 300 MB of text operators took 33 s and 1.7 GB. The real statements have at most 219 items per page and read in well under a second, so the bounds leave a wide margin.
rejected: No bounds beyond file size and page count.
Parsing in a worker of our own (the bounds make the main-thread work small).
source: owner-request: coordinator, review round of the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Purchase dates must be plausible
decisions.decision: A purchase date after its booking date, or more than 366 days before it, refuses the statement with the control named and both dates. Value dates are not compared with purchase dates (Q-209).
decisions.why: The purchase date decides the budget period of the transaction (D-128); a misread or misprinted year would put it in a period years away while every amount still adds up.
rejected: Accepting any date.
Clamping a wrong date to the booking date.
